sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title: Hagberg 1993/2006 (already held by the project from the mayo1264/capa1241/huas1242 search; copied to the wara1303 folder). Its Warao section (pp. 19-21, 137-139) is second-hand from Osborn 1966 and confirms the catalog: penult primary, alternating secondary leftward, odd-syllable words with unstressed initial, a few final/antepenult exceptions. Beyond the item list, two first-hand sources were reached. (a) Romero-Figueroa 1997, A Reference Grammar of Warao, p. 112 — open Rosetta Project excerpt on archive.org, downloaded and page-image verified: penult 'almost without exception', secondary on alternate syllables counting back, example (309) matching the catalog rule string, stress non-contrastive; recommended as the new deciding quote (first-hand, replacing the second-hand Hayes 1980 quote). (b) Osborn 1966 (IJAL 32(2):108-123, DOI 10.1086/464890) — paywalled; archive.org lending copy restricted, but its stress section was reconstructed from FTS snippets: same penult + alternating pattern, plus refinements the catalog does not record (antepenult = third vowel from the end .aeCV/..aiCV/..oiCV words, antepenult in onomatopoeic particles, one contrastive penult/antepenult pair, final stress in Spanish loans). Osborn 1966 full text remains high priority (online with a university library loginper). all lookups were done with archive.org/Crossref APIs by automated download.

new_statements.quote: The predominant pattern of heavy stress is on the penultimate vowel, antepenultimate heavy stress remaining confined to some onomatopoeic words and ultimate heavy stress to Spanish loans which are heavily stressed in the ultimate syllable in that language. Heavy stress almost without exception falls on the second syllable from the end in disyllables, trisllables and polysyllables. [...] (309) nahóro; nàhoró-te 'You eat'; nahòro-náka 'You do not eat'; nàhorò-naká-ra 'Don't you eat?' The marking of weak stress in (309) agrees with a rule by which alternate syllables are stressed with weak secondary stress, counting back from the heavily stressed syllable, and syllables not stressed with heavy stress are unstressed. In Warao, no two words are distinguished by placement of stress.

new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate primary stress with alternating secondary stresses running leftward from the penult (initial syllable unstressed in odd-syllable words, as (309) shows: 010, 1010, 01010, 101010); stress is non-contrastive and re-aligns to the penult under suffixation. Antepenult and final stress are confined to onomatopoeia and Spanish loans. This is a first-hand grammar statement that confirms the catalog's fixed-strict penult coding and its rule string exactly.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable; secondary stresses on every other syllable to the left of it (syllabic trochees built right to left, initial syllable of odd-syllable words unstressed): 10, 010, 1010, 01010, 101010, 0101010, 10101010. Syllable weight plays no role. Data are Osborn 1966's, cited second-hand.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'secondary stress occurs on every other syllable preceding primary stress' (grave accents in ex. (2)/(3)); odd-syllable words leave the initial syllable unstressed (koránu, yiwàranáe); in exceptional words the alternating secondaries count leftward from wherever primary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: Per Osborn 1966, a few words carry primary stress on the final or the antepenultimate syllable. Hagberg (p. 137 fn. 2) attributes exceptional final stress to a lexical accent on the final syllable and the antepenultimate cases to morphology (certain suffixes entering the derivation after foot-building); in ch. 1 (p. 19) he says Hayes would presumably use lexical accent and/or extrametricality for them.
new_statements.identity_note: Hagberg names no dialect; his Warao data are Osborn 1966's ('a language of Venezuela'). Romero-Figueroa 1997's data (the existing statement) come from Caño Buna / Caño Manamo in the Orinoco delta. No variety-level discrepancy arises.

sources.note: First-hand (fieldwork 1987-89, 1993; Caño Buna/Manamo): primary ('heavy') stress on the penultimate syllable almost without exception; secondary stress on alternate syllables counting leftward from the primary; antepenult only in some onomatopoeic words, final only in Spanish loans; stress shifts rightward under suffixation to stay penultimate; stress is purely delimitative, never contrastive. Example (309) instantiates exactly the catalog rule string: 010 (nahóro), 1010 (nàhoró-te), 01010 (nahòro-náka), 101010 (nàhorò-naká-ra). Accents verified on the page scan.
sources.venue: LINCOM Studies in Native American Linguistics 6

sources.quote: In Warao, stress iterates on even-numbered syllables right-to-left, with primary stress on the rightmost syllable. In both cases, a foot-based analysis straightforwardly posits quantity-insensitive trochees, and the direction of foot alignment matches that of primary-stress alignment (left for Pintupi, right for Warao). This results in a fixed position for the primary stress (initial in Pintupi, penult in Warao).

sources.quote: Primary stress in Warao falls on the penultimate syllable in most words, and secondary stress occurs on every other syllable preceding primary stress, as illustrated in (2). (2) Warao (Osborn 1966): tíra woman; apáu well placed; koránu drink it!; rúhunáe he sat down; yiwàranáe he finished it; nàhoròahàkutái the one who ate; yàpurùkitànehás e verily to climb. [...] (3) Stress Assignment in Warao: (a) Build syllabic feet iteratively from right to left. (b) Insert * in each foot and link from left to right. [...] any word that has an odd number of syllables will end up with an unfooted initial syllable [...] koránu. (fn. 2) Osborn reports a few instances of primary stress occurring on the final syllable or on the antepenultimate syllable, but the alternating secondary stresses are always determined by the placement of primary stress.

sources.note: Second-hand (Osborn 1966 data): primary stress penultimate in most words, secondary on every other syllable to the left, initial syllable of odd-syllable words unstressed (no degenerate feet); a few final- and antepenult-stressed exceptions, which Hagberg attributes to lexical accent on the final syllable and to morphology (suffixes entering after foot-building). Analysis: left-stressed syllabic (trochaic) feet built right-to-left, same as Hayes 1991. Accent marks in the scanned text are partly garbled; the pattern statement in prose is clean.
sources.venue: An Autosegmental Theory of Stress

sources.quote: Monosyllabic words have a single stressed syllable. Strong stress may occur on the ultimate syllable, the penultimate syllable or the antepenultimate syllable. [...] The predominant pattern of strong stress is on the penultimate vowel. The syllable following a strong penultimate stress is weakly stressed: nihaérapáka alligator, koránu drink it! [...] Of the remaining syllables of the word, alternate syllables are stressed with a weaker secondary stress, counting back from the strongly stressed syllable. [...] Thus the predominant syllable stress pattern of words is trochaic. [...] In words with odd-numbered syllables the pattern is trochaic with an extra weakly stressed initial syllable: enàhoròahakutái the one who [...] Strong stress is always antepenult if the pattern of the word is either ....aeCV, or ....aiCV, or ....oiCV [...] the strong stress falls on the third vowel from the end of the word. [...] Strong stress is always antepenult in a small subclass of particles which are onomatopoetic [...] Strong stress is either penult or antepenult in two pairs of sequences. In the first pair stress is contrastive. [...] Spanish loans with final stress, especially personal names, ret…
